name: Femi Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ride a moped for two food apps in the city centre, mostly the lunch rush and then five till eleven at night. I've done it six years, so I'm one of the riders the restaurant staff wave through, and I run the riders' group chat for the Market Street area. I know which kitchens are slow, which flats have broken lifts, and where you can park without a ticket. What wears me out is the app changing pay rates on a Tuesday night with no warning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The streets, honestly. When the city's lit up and I'm moving well, it's the best job I've had. I live with my partner Sanne, she's a nurse on nights, so we pass each other in the hallway and that suits us fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now maybe people will stop talking about robots and start talking about our pay. The apps already use software to set our rates, so for us the hype was never the robot, it was the algorithm. I'd post that in the group chat straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my real problem stays my real problem. The app cut the base fare on Market Street twice this year, and no hype about AI changes that. I'd still be one rate change away from a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding the same shifts and keep pushing the riders' group to join the couriers' branch of the union. I'd also keep putting a hundred a month into savings, because I've got about three months covered and I want four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady but tired. Nothing dramatic, just the same grind and the same worry about pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the algorithm is the real issue. Can you give me a moment when you felt that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last March they changed how distance is counted, and my Friday went from ninety to sixty for the same hours. Nobody told us. I only found out because three riders messaged me asking if their app was broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes with AI, what would you want to change anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A minimum rate per hour logged in, not per drop. Sanne laughs because I say it at dinner every week, but it's the one thing that would make this a proper job.

say: The **algorithm**, not the robot, was always the real threat to riders like me.
Now that the hype has passed, let's finally **talk about pay** for couriers.
think: My biggest risk stays the same: one **rate change** can wreck a month.
Without a **minimum hourly rate**, this job never feels secure, even with no AI shake-up.
do: Keep riding the **same shifts** in the city centre for both food apps.
Push the riders' group chat to **join the union** branch for couriers.
Add **£100 a month** to savings to get from three to four months covered.
feel: **Tired but steady**, carrying the same pay worry he already had.
S0.quote: The app cut the base fare on Market Street twice this year, and no hype about AI changes that.
fieldNote: He sees the **pay algorithm** as the AI that already affects him, so hype or no hype changes little.
A sudden **Friday pay drop** last March still shapes how he talks about the job.
His **partner's nursing income** steadies the household, but he still wants his own cushion bigger.

steps.text: Keep riding lunch and evening shifts on both food apps
Sign up the Market Street riders to the couriers' union branch
Put £100 a month into savings until four months are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same story as always: the firms save money and the workers carry the risk. If the apps start using AI to answer customers and plan routes, fine, but they'll use it to squeeze us too. I'd want the union in the room when they roll it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the riding itself is safe for a while. But the dispatch side, the support chat, the stuff that already decides who gets which order, that gets sharper and colder. When the app is smarter than the dispatcher, there's nobody left to argue with about a bad order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the bike, because I'm good at it and there are still jobs. I'd get more serious with the union, go to the branch meetings instead of just reading the minutes, and write down every pay change in a notebook so we have proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not losing the job tomorrow, but I can feel the ground tilting under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep a notebook. Why on paper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust apps to keep records against apps. I've got a red notebook in the moped box already with every rate I've seen since 2023. It's not clever, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new riders, the students on bicycles. They don't know the tricks yet, and if support is all chatbots, nobody tells them they can dispute a fine. I end up doing that job for free.

say: Firms will use AI to **save money** while riders carry the **risk**.
The union should be **in the room** whenever apps roll out new AI tools.
think: The riding stays mine, but **dispatch and support** get colder and harder to challenge.
There'll be **nobody to argue with** when a smart app hands out bad orders.
do: Stay on the **moped** in the same area, because the riding work still exists.
Start going to **union branch meetings** instead of only reading the minutes.
Log every pay change in his **red notebook** as proof for disputes.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if the ground under the job is slowly tilting.
S1.quote: When the app is smarter than the dispatcher, there's nobody left to argue with about a bad order.
fieldNote: He separates the **riding**, which feels safe, from the **app management**, which he sees getting worse.
He refuses digital records out of **distrust**, and keeps a paper log instead.
He already acts as **unpaid support** for newer riders, and expects that load to grow.

steps.text: Keep riding the Market Street area at the same hours
Attend the couriers' union branch meeting every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need public rules now, not later. A basic income, limits on what the platforms can do, something. I'd be the loud one in the group chat saying we've got two years before the thinking part is gone and five before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it scares me. The app is already the boss, and in 2028 it's a boss that never sleeps. I'd probably have three years of riding left after that, but I'd spend those three years watching the delivery robots get tested on my own streets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Sanne about moving to her hospital as a porter or a care assistant, because that's people work. I'd push savings hard, cutting the takeaways we ironically never cook at home, and I'd go on any march for a basic income. I wouldn't learn AI tools, though. That's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and angry that nobody would have prepared. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have three years more than an office worker. Does that feel like a head start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Three years is long enough to watch it coming but too short to train for anything big. I'd use it to save and to switch into the hospital, not to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn AI tools. Even if it would help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it sounds stubborn. But I'd rather move into a job where a person is the point, like helping patients, than learn to babysit the thing that's replacing me.

say: We need **public rules** and a **basic income** now, before the platforms move.
Riders have two years before thinking AI arrives and about **five** before robots do.
think: The app becomes a **boss that never sleeps** once AGI arrives in 2028.
His last **three years of riding** would feel like watching his own replacement being tested.
do: Ask about **porter or care assistant** jobs at his partner's hospital.
Cut **takeaway spending** at home and push savings as hard as possible.
Join every **march** for a basic income and limits on platforms.
feel: **Scared** about how little time there is.
**Angry** that nobody would have prepared riders for it.
S2.quote: I'd spend those three years watching the delivery robots get tested on my own streets.
fieldNote: The extra **three years** before robots feels to him like a countdown, not a head start.
He rejects **AI tools** and looks for work where a person is the point.
His progressive outlook shows in calls for a **basic income** and platform rules.

steps.text: Apply for porter or care assistant jobs at Sanne's hospital
Stop ordering takeaways and cook at home to save more
Join marches calling for a basic income and platform limits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if governments use it, and nothing if they don't. I'd be pushing the union to win a deal now: retraining paid by the platforms, and notice before robots come onto our routes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd keep riding until about 2031 and then the app side gets taken over completely. The robots come around 2034, so I'd be in my early thirties when the riding goes. That's young enough to change, but I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a care course at the college in the evenings, maybe in the second year, while still riding. Sanne says there's always a shortage of care assistants on her ward. I'd keep the union work going and keep saving, so I could take a pay cut while I train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning anxious. There's time, but the end is the same, and I know myself, I'd leave it late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave it late. What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first robot doing a real drop on Market Street. Honestly, that's what it would take. I won't believe the robots are coming until one rolls past me with a pizza.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if you took a pay cut to train?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The moped upgrade I've been saving for. I'd ride the old one into the ground and keep that money for the months on care-assistant pay.

say: Five years is **enough time** only if governments actually use it.
Platforms should **pay for retraining** and give notice before robots take routes.
think: The **riding** probably lasts until about 2034, when he'd be in his early thirties.
He's young enough to **change careers**, but he'd hate leaving the streets.
do: Start an **evening care course** at the college in the second year, while still riding.
Keep **union work** going for a platform-funded retraining deal.
Save the **moped upgrade money** to cover months on lower trainee pay.
feel: **Uneasy turning anxious**, because the end point doesn't change.
**Worried about himself** leaving the change too late.
S3.quote: I won't believe the robots are coming until one rolls past me with a pizza.
fieldNote: He admits he'd **wait for proof**, like the first robot on his street, before moving.
A **care course** is his realistic route, tied to his partner's ward.
Even with five years, the **same end point** keeps him from feeling secure.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening care course at the college
Press the union for a platform-funded retraining deal
Skip the moped upgrade and bank the money instead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly. Put a tax on the robot fleets, fund training, make sure riders aren't just dropped. I'd be saying that at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels far away. I'd ride till my mid-thirties, which was always roughly my plan anyway. The worry is that I'd get comfortable and do nothing until 2036, when the apps change overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding and keep saving at the same rate. Around year three or four I'd start the care course properly, while riding fewer evenings. I'd want the union to push for a robot tax by the end of the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but still uneasy. The road ends, just further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new rider starting today in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the city, save every month, and have a second trade ready before the robots are cheaper than your moped. That's what I'd want someone to tell me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Sanne's job change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a lot. Nursing is people work, so in this one her job feels safer than mine. Knowing that, I could take a risk on training, because one of us would still be steady.

say: Ten years gives a **real chance** to make the change fair for riders.
A **robot tax** should pay for training so riders aren't just dropped.
think: Riding until his **mid-thirties** was roughly his plan anyway.
His real risk is getting **comfortable** and doing nothing until 2036.
do: Keep **riding and saving** at the same rate for the first few years.
Start the **care course** properly in year three or four, with fewer evening shifts.
Push the union for a **robot tax** by the end of the decade.
feel: **Calmer** than in the faster pictures, but still **uneasy** about the end.
S4.quote: Learn the city, save every month, and have a second trade ready before the robots are cheaper than your moped.
fieldNote: His **partner's nursing job** looks safer here, which lets him consider a training risk.
He names **complacency** as his own weak point.
His advice to new riders shows a **practical** streak under the political talk.

steps.text: Keep riding both food apps and saving £100 a month
Start a care assistant course in year three
Back union calls for a tax on robot delivery fleets

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't time for anything, and the robots would arrive while I'm still saving. What would help is the platforms paying into a fund for riders, and a hospital or care job with a training wage I could actually live on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Riders like me never get asked before the app changes, so why would anyone ask us before the robots come? That's the whole thing for me.

headlineQuote: Riders like me never get asked before the app changes, so why would anyone ask us before the robots come?
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old moped rider** who has worked two food apps in the city centre for six years.
He runs the **riders' group chat** and acts as unofficial support for newer riders.
He sees the **pay algorithm** as the AI that already hurts him, and keeps a paper log of rates.
He avoids **AI tools** and leans towards care work at his partner's hospital as an exit.
His mood rises from **uneasy** to **alarmed** as the AGI warning time shrinks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because two years leaves no time to save or retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **platform-funded fund** for riders, and a care job with a **training wage** he could live on.
